title: "Words and mind turn back from it" (2.4)
hook: the Taittiriya names the bliss of Brahman, and in the same breath says words can't reach it

segments.voice: Yesterday: understanding, and the bliss at the center. Your line was the innermost is joy.

Someone you love comes back from the hospital holding a newborn, and you ask, so, what's it like? They open their mouth. They close it. They try again: it's, you know. It's just. Then they give up and hand you the baby. That small failure is its own kind of answer: some things are real enough to change your life and still too big to fit in a sentence. The Taittiriya Upanishad has spent a whole chapter mapping the layers of a person, food, breath, mind, understanding, bliss. And right in the middle of the map, it stops and admits something.
screen: `SO, WHAT'S IT LIKE?` → `IT'S, YOU KNOW. IT'S JUST.` → `THE MAP ADMITS SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse in Sanskrit: yato vaco nivartante aprapya manasa saha. From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having reached it. Then the second half: the one who knows the bliss of Brahman is never afraid. The picture in nivartante is turning around, coming home. Words set out toward Brahman and come back without arriving. The mind goes with them, and comes back too. Notice the text doesn't say Brahman is nothing, or that the search is pointless. It says the search comes back changed. And it doesn't throw words away. The very next lines go straight on to the next layer, the self made of understanding. The Upanishad keeps talking, carefully, about the thing it says talk can't hold. That's not a contradiction. It's how a signpost works. The sign isn't the town, but it tells you which way to walk. You met this move a few days ago in the Brihadaranyaka: neti, neti, not this, not this. There, words fall away one by one. Here, they turn around on their own. And then there's the promise about fear. The text says, a little later in the chapter, that fear comes when a person makes even a small gap, a sense of separation, inside this. Know the bliss, and there's no gap to be afraid of. The verse comes back near the end of the chapter, with a line added: such a person isn't tormented by the thought, why didn't I do the good, why did I do the wrong.
screen: `WORDS SET OUT, AND TURN BACK.` · `THE MIND TURNS BACK WITH THEM.` · `A SIGNPOST, NOT THE TOWN.` · `KNOW THE BLISS; NO FEAR.` · then, large: `YATO VACO NIVARTANTE.`

segments.voice: Pick one sound in the room, a fan, traffic, your own breath, and notice how fast the mind names it; then let the name go and stay with the sound itself, before the label. When a word arrives, and it will, let it turn back on its own, and return to just hearing, the moment before the word.
Nivartante, they turn back. Yato vaco nivartante: the Taittiriya's way of saying Brahman's bliss can be known but not captured in speech.
Your line: beyond words. In the Taittiriya, Brahman's bliss can be known, not captured. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: This verse is often chanted in Vedanta classes and recitations of the Taittiriya's second chapter, the Brahmanandavalli, and teachers use it to explain why Brahman is pointed to rather than described.

fork.reveal: the next lines go right on to describe the self made of understanding. the text points with words while saying words turn back.

original.note: Sanskrit: "from which words turn back." ni + vṛt, to turn back, return.

chat.says: If words turn back from Brahman, why does the Upanishad keep talking about it?
options: It keeps pointing carefully, like a signpost: not the town, but the way.
Because the text says the right words can capture Brahman completely.
It stops talking right there; the rest of the chapter is silent.
chat.meaning: Yato vaco nivartante: words and mind turn back without reaching it. Yet the text keeps speaking carefully, pointing the way like a signpost.
